query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of a Group IV element (such as Ti) into the equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy will improve its room‐temperature ductility by enhancing grain boundary cohesion and disrupting the continuous brittle bonding network, while largely preserving its high‐temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy produced by conventional vacuum arc melting and homogenization, exhibiting excellent high-temperature mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very limited tensile ductility at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy by substituting a minor fraction (e.g., approximately 5–10 atomic percent) of one of the constituent elements with titanium (or by doping trace Ti into the alloy) so that the overall BCC solid solution is retained.
generation.conditions: The modified alloy will be fabricated via vacuum arc melting followed by appropriate homogenization and thermomechanical processing to ensure a uniform single-phase BCC structure. Mechanical testing is conducted at room temperature (for ductility assessment), at 1600 °C (to verify high-temperature mechanical performance), and under relevant irradiation conditions (using ion irradiation at elevated temperatures to simulate service conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: A more homogeneous BCC microstructure with improved grain boundary cohesion and a subtle change in local atomic bonding due to Ti’s larger atomic radius and different d-electron character.
generation.mechanism: Ti addition is expected to reduce the intrinsic brittleness by promoting more effective dislocation motion and reducing grain boundary decohesion at low temperature, without substantially altering the high melting point and lattice stability that govern high-temperature strength or the defect energetics that underpin irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The intervention should result in a marked improvement of room-temperature ductility (i.e. increased plastic strain before failure) with minimal changes in the yield strength at 1600 °C and with maintained or only slightly modified irradiation resistance compared to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline.
generation.baseline: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy that is known to be very brittle at room temperature while showing excellent mechanical strength at 1600 °C and having irradiation resistance predicted by first-principles calculations.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only for a minor (trace to low) level of Ti addition. Excessive Ti levels may destabilize the single-phase BCC structure or induce unwanted intermetallic phases, which could compromise high-temperature performance and irradiation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: Exact improvement in ductility, the optimal Ti content, and long-term irradiation behavior need to be quantified experimentally. The interplay between slight compositional change and phase stability requires careful validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of modified RHEAs by preparing NbMoTaW alloys with incremental Ti additions (e.g., 0, 5, and 10 at% Ti, with Ti substituting for one of the refractory elements) using vacuum arc melting and standardized homogenization/thermomechanical processing. Characterize the microstructure via XRD and electron microscopy to confirm the retention of a single-phase BCC solid solution. Conduct tensile tests at room temperature to quantify ductility, perform high-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical tests to confirm strength retention, and run ion irradiation experiments at elevated temperature to assess irradiation resistance.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile strain to failure (ductility percentage)
Yield strength and stress–strain behavior at 1600 °C
Microstructural analysis (phase and grain boundary stability) before and after irradiation
Irradiation-induced defect density and hardness/hardening behavior
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Ti addition does not significantly increase room-temperature ductility (e.g., improvement in plastic strain less than an expected threshold of about 10% relative increase) or if it causes a measurable deterioration (more than ~5% reduction) in the high-temperature mechanical strength or a marked decrease in irradiation resistance compared to the baseline NbMoTaW, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory HEAs (RHEAs) stand out among various types of HEAs due to their unparalleled mechanical properties at high temperatures exceeding 800 °C, and even up to 1500 °C in some cases [,], making them viable options for high-temperature structural applications, outperforming typical Ni-based superalloys. Refractory high-entropy alloys, thanks to their high strength at high temperatures, high melting point, and high hardness brought by their resistance to friction and wear properties, may be used in aerospace engines, gas turbines, and the nuclear irradiation field. However, the reported literature has primarily centered on compression deformation investigations. For most RHEAs, due to their room-temperature brittleness, their tensile ductility is commonly negligible []. Therefore, improving the room-temperature plasticity of RHEAs is the premise of its high-temperature application.

Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.
